Digital Cocaine

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Digital dementia...juvenile alzheimers. Author Brad Huddleston speaks about his latest book "Digital Cocaine" that reveals distrurbing new research about how screens rewire our brains

Summary:
It would be normal to expect anxiety, emotional outbursts, restlessness, craving, memory loss and a lack of focus in someone dealing with a drug addiction. But television, multimedia producer and tech expert BRAD HUDDLESTON has penned “DIGITAL COCAINE” bringing together the latest brain science from researchers around the world that shows how extended screen use – television, tablets and smart phones – rewires the brain and causes new brain pathologies, psychiatric conditions and addiction, particularly (but not only) in children. We speak to Huddleston on his visit to South Africa, where he is addressing schools, churches and universities, appealing for iBalance in a world that is rapidly reaching screen saturation.

Tabitha Lage

Press Release:


Digital Cocaine
It would be normal to expect anxiety, emotional outbursts, restlessness and memory loss in someone dealing with a drug addiction. But disturbing new research reveals that extended screen use – tablets, computers and television – could rewire the brain, causing similar brain pathologies and psychiatric conditions in children and adults. Carte Blanche meets tech expert Brad Huddlestone, who appeals for balance in a rapidly-changing digital world.


Script:


PROMOS SCRIPT

10 secs:
VO: Are you always online? Do you struggle to step away from your phone or computer screen? Disturbing new research shows that addiction to digital devices is hurting the brain…

15 secs:
VO: Your child’s mental health could be at risk if you haven’t set boundaries in their digital life.
BRAD HUDDLESTON: they’re tired of the depression that sets in, they’re tired of the anxiety that sets in…
VO: New research reveals the brain pathologies emerging from the digital tsunami.

15 secs:
VO: From cell phones to computer screens, new brain science is sounding alarm bells about digital addiction…
UPS BRAD IN PRESENTATION: When this tsunami of technology swept over us…we just didn’t know the unintended consequences would develop.


STORY SCRIPT

The Lage family from Fourways, Johannesburg was excited when the little ones got tablets from their grandparents for Christmas. But, things soon seemed to get out of hand. Tabitha realised her son struggled to set boundaries around his digital playtime.

TABITHA: It started to become a fight – so Tyler would start playing on the tablet and to get him off the tablet was a concern for me.

The family had already decided to do away with their television because they saw the addictive effect it had on their children.

TABITHA: Once again that whole addiction with children watching TV constantly, being glued to the TV, not getting their attention…

Tabitha and her husband rely on screens and social media to make a living – but they’ve become aware that screens hold the potential to harm their children.

And as counter-cultural as their stance might seem – they are not alone in kicking back. One man has made it life’s mission to bring to light the destructive side of screens.

UPS BRAD IN PRESENTATION: I’ve just released Digital Cocaine about five days ago – it’s subtitled a journey into iBalance…

With degrees in computer science and theology, Brad Huddleston travels the world to research the science behind screen addiction and help people.

UPS BRAD IN PRESENTATION: Some of this information just three years ago we were totally unaware of the things that were going on – so when this tsunami of technology swept over us, particularly in 2007 when the first iPhone was realeased, we just didn’t know the unintended consequences would develop.

This is Brad’s desk at home – he shows it to audiences to explain that he actually values and uses technology. But it has burned him. He counsels children and adults and helps law enforcement grasp what science is starting to show.

DEREK: NOW YOU ARE EQUATING DIGITAL ADDICTION TO COCAINE USE – ISN’T THAT MELODRAMATIC?

BRAD: The neuroscience compares it to cocaine – they are the ones that are studying the chemicals in the brain and the brain scans and they can show where the brain lights up with certain activities.so when you look at a person who’s addicted to pornography for instance the same areas in their brain of anticipation and addiction light up as a cocaine and heroin addict.

Brad says all that distinguishes South Africa from the world is that we’re slightly behind the curve in rolling out individual screens at schools.

UPS FROM PRESENTATION AT SCHOOL: Last year a four-year old created international headlines by becoming Britain’s youngest iPad addict…

Brad takes his audiences on a journey into the published literature on neuroscience and into the brain itself.

The nucleus accumbens is where a chemical called dopamine induces pleasure.

BRAD: It’s also known in layman’s terms as the pleasure centre – it’s all about pleasure…we text, we social media, we do this because we like these little hits of dopamine, which is a neurotransmitter hitting that pleasure centre and we derive pleasure – there’s nothing wrong with dopamine but some activities generate more than others.

And when we generate too much dopamine, whether by cocaine, alcohol or screens, the brain starts to defend itself against being overstressed and overdosed. It builds a chemical barrier to push out the dopamine. But we don’t like the good feeling being cut off and so we do more of the activity for longer to try and penetrate the barrier and get the dopamine over that wall again.

Science now has names for conditions flowing from screen addiction, like FOMO = the fear of missing out, or NOMOPHOBIA = phone separation anxiety… - all psychological conditions that hamper personal wellbeing and relationships.

DEREK: YOU TALK ABOUT DIGITAL DEMENTIA BUT YOU’RE NOT TALKING ABOUT OLD-TIMERS?
BRAD: That term comes from South Korea – South Korea is the most wired nation on this planet – they have the fastest internet. Their gaming community sprung up before anyone. As a result of their super-saturation, they have had to contrast 200 digital detox rehabilitation centres across their small country and one of the conditions that the doctors there have discovered is memory loss in children. It mimics Alzheimer’s.

DION: In mainland China there are about 300 already operating and this is really for gamers and there’s stories about boot camps – they’re on YouTube…they’re funny but very sad as well…

DEREK’S LINK: Dion Chang has always had his finger on the pulse of global change – but his personal experience with burnout has led to a whole new field of study.

DION: They’ve got incidents of gamers who are actually wearing adult nappies so that they can game 36 hours straight without going to the toilet, so it gets that bad.

Producers of the 2013 documentary Web Junkie gained access to a Chinese digital boot camp and featured the Chinese government's classification of internet addiction as a clinical disorder. In the west, the latest Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM5) has only recently listed Internet Addiction as a condition needing further research.

UPS WEB JUNKIE MOVIE: Do you realise what kind of a place you’re at now? It seems you have failed to perceive what reality is. What did you do? “I used the internet”.

As one of South Africa’s top corporate trends analysts, Dion suffered digital burnout from his ‘always on’, ‘always available’ lifestyle. As he sought strategies to cope, his firm began to probe what this phenomenon might mean for local business.

DION: Mobile addiction is interesting – it manifests itself differently for men and women. For men it was more cardio stress related heart attacks, that kind of thing and for women, depression.

DEREK: But surely business isn’t really interested in our little “burnouts”?

DION: People who burn down go for weeks at a time so it’s a serious threat to human resources …it’s almost like a nervous breakdown that you experience.

DION LINK: Brad has found that everywhere he speaks to young people there’s an alarming incidence of self-harm, like cutting. And he sees a link with digital addiction.

Over time repetitive, hard screen use causes the protective barrier in the brain to get so strong that it becomes harder for dopamine to get through to the pleasure centre.
Again, the focus is on the young brain’s pleasure centre. Repetitive screen use strengthens that protective barrier in the brain so dopamine can’t get through and activate this area.
The above is repetition of what you already explained in the same way earlier in script hence my changes – agree?

BRAD: It goes numb, so now you’ve got a personality change, you can’t feel properly and that is anhedonia…and unlike the other conditions like FOMO and digital dementia, that one has been around for a while but it’s been associated with schizophrenics, people with major depressive disorders and severe drug addicts and now they’re finding anhedonia in children – because it has been induced by the overuse of technology.

Brad says many children who approach him after his talks, confess that they self-harm just to feel something. Over half the children in audiences we saw him speak to, indicated they knew someone who self-harmed.

BRAD: The digital component is that they’ve overdone it, they’ve numbed the pleasure centre and now they’re tricking a different chemical to come is – but the danger is that you build up tolerance to that to the self-harm gets worse as well.

DEREK’s LINK: Many studies focus on internet or gaming addiction but Brad goes much further – he says that digital multitasking at all levels is where the problem begins.

BRAD: Our brains are actually sequential processors, they can only do one thing at a time… we can, though, task-switch tasks so quickly that it creates the illusion of multitasking, but the brain is actually switching. When they’re doing homework most often they’re doing a lot of other things that is outpacing their homework and it is causing the grades around the world to decrease…that is very unnatural for the brain, it’s very stressful for the brain and is causing chemical changes.

DION: The minute your preciousness has a notification you drop what you’re doing you go to that and you keep jumping from thing to thing. We try to do so many things that we don’t allow that short term memory to transfer to long-term memory. So that’s why we don’t recall anything. When people come into meetings on their devices and I call it “No really I’m listening” – you actually don’t recall…it’s those small peripheral activities that start impacting on the efficiency of an organisation.

As with any addiction, the way forward can be tough. Some Randburg Hoerskool seniors admitted Brad had opened their eyes – especially about multi-tasking’s impact on sleep.
ANDRE: We have an iPad with a Kindle app so I read books and so I read sometimes when I read the book till at night, and put it down, I can’t sleep – it’s like an hour before I start to doze off.
CHANE: Two years ago when Candy Crush came out, the I would play Candy Crush when I should be studying …and then when I would go to be I would play it and then when I close my eyes I can still see the little candies – so it does get really bad and so I think might as well stay up and play it.
Brad doesn’t apologise for recommending tough love…And, many top IT executives are known to be low-tech parents that favour little to no screen-use in their homes.

Don’t put your baby in front of a screen. Think hard about putting toddlers in front of one and yes, television is a screen. Remove technology from bedrooms. Get 9-and-a-quarter hours sleep. Get out. Exercise.

DION: The golden rule is then minutes before ten minutes before the hour you step away and you don’t step away to check your social media, step away, breathe some air – do something

DEREK: Smell the roses…

DION: non-digital – re-learn to monotask.

DEREK: I mean that is a big ask, Brad?

BRAD: I think you saw today from the reaction of those kids and how many stayed after and this happens nearly everywhere I go…they know that something is off…about this – they’re tired of the depression that sets in, they’re tired of the anxiety that sets in – they’ll get desperate enough to do it and they do come back sometimes some of them will tell me man I feel so much better or parents who have enforced that will tell me it’s so good to have my child back. So yes, it’s difficult because it’s so much a part of our culture.

DEREK: It’s a big step…

BRAD: But if you get desperate enough, you will do it.

metadata.Summary: It would be normal to expect anxiety, emotional outbursts, restlessness, craving, memory loss and a lack of focus in someone dealing with a drug addiction. But television, multimedia producer and tech expert BRAD HUDDLESTON has penned “DIGITAL COCAINE” bringing together the latest brain science from researchers around the world that shows how extended screen use – television, tablets and smart phones – rewires the brain and causes new brain pathologies, psychiatric conditions and addiction, particularly (but not only) in children. We speak to Huddleston on his visit to South Africa, where he is addressing schools, churches and universities, appealing for iBalance in a world that is rapidly reaching screen saturation.
